why_this_tool: AWS Bedrock is the right tool to practise with because it puts models from several providers behind one identity, quota and billing system and one Converse message format, which is exactly the surface a platform team owns.
alternatives: Claude API direct (newest model features first, but separate keys and billing outside AWS identity), OpenAI API and Gemini API (single-provider endpoints with their own message formats and quotas), and LiteLLM (a self-hosted gateway that puts one OpenAI-style interface, budgets and routing in front of all of them, including Bedrock).

setup.do: Create an AWS identity with Bedrock permissions and local credentials, noting that Bedrock is a paid cloud service billed per token and that the closest local substitute is replaying recorded responses through a stubbed SDK client.
setup.done_when: Your terminal can authenticate to AWS and the identity is allowed to invoke a Bedrock model.
setup.why: Every later step calls Bedrock under this identity, so access is the first thing a platform engineer has to own. Keeping prompts tiny holds the cost to a few cents, and the stub lets you rerun the path offline.

setup.do: Install the Python AWS SDK (boto3) in a fresh virtual environment and set a default region.
setup.done_when: A Python session can create a Bedrock runtime client in your chosen region without an error.
setup.why: The lesson drives Bedrock from application code, and a clean environment is what you will pin later for CI.

setup.do: Pick one inexpensive text model that is available in your region and supports the Converse API, tool use and streaming.
setup.done_when: You have written down one model identifier and the region you will use for the whole path.
setup.why: Model availability and feature support differ by region and by model, and a wrong pick shows up later as confusing validation errors.

steps.do: Run the quickstart inference request against your chosen model (paid AWS call; save the response to replay through a stubbed client when offline).
steps.done_when: The model's text reply is printed in your terminal.
steps.why: A first successful call proves that credentials, region and model access all line up before you add any complexity.

steps.do: Compare the APIs Bedrock supports and write a short note on which one your application contract will use and why.
steps.done_when: Your note names the chosen API, the endpoint it runs on, and one API you ruled out with the reason.

steps.why: Bedrock exposes the same foundation models through several APIs and endpoints, and the platform team must choose one contract for application code instead of letting every team pick its own.

steps.do: Write a multi-turn conversation with the Converse API, appending each assistant reply to the messages list before the next user turn.
steps.done_when: The model's third reply correctly refers to something said in the first turn.

source.title: Inference using Converse API - Amazon Bedrock

steps.why: The messages structure is the core object model of Converse, and the service is stateless, so your code owns the conversation history.

steps.do: Configure a system prompt and explicit inference parameters, then run the same user message under two system prompts and compare the outputs.
steps.done_when: You have two saved outputs that differ only because the system prompt changed.

source.title: Inference using Converse API - Amazon Bedrock

steps.why: Treating the system prompt and inference settings as explicit, separate inputs is the first step toward prompts that can be tested rather than strings buried in code.

steps.do: Create a prompt with variables in Prompt management, then run inference on that prompt resource through Converse by filling the variables at call time.
steps.done_when: A Converse call that references the prompt resource and passes variable values returns a reply, with no prompt text in your code.

verified.section_found: Run inference on a prompt resource from Prompt management

steps.why: A prompt stored as a versioned resource can be reviewed, tested and rolled back independently of application deploys.

steps.do: Configure one tool in the tool configuration and write the loop that runs the tool locally and sends the result back to the model.
steps.done_when: The model requests your tool, your code returns a result, and the final reply uses that result.

source.title: Inference using Converse API - Amazon Bedrock

steps.why: Tool use is a multi-step exchange your code must drive, and Converse gives it one schema across providers.

steps.do: Run the same request with ConverseStream and print each text delta as it arrives.
steps.done_when: Text appears incrementally in your terminal and you see a final stop event with a stop reason.

verified.section_found: Send a message to a model and stream the response.

steps.why: Streaming changes perceived latency and the error handling your gateway needs, because the response arrives as a sequence of events instead of one body.

steps.do: Query the token usage and latency metrics from each response and log them as one structured line per call.
steps.done_when: Your log shows input tokens, output tokens and latency in milliseconds for at least five calls.
steps.why: Cost and latency are only manageable once every call records its tokens and timing, and Converse returns both in the response.

steps.do: Write retry handling with backoff for the throttling and service errors that Converse can return, and test it by sending a burst of concurrent requests (or by stubbing a throttling error locally).
steps.done_when: A throttled request is retried and succeeds, and your log shows the retry count.
steps.why: Quota limits surface as specific errors, and well-behaved clients are what keep one noisy caller from taking down a shared account.

steps.do: Write a thin gateway function that every caller goes through, which attaches request metadata naming the calling team and use case to each Converse request.
steps.done_when: Two callers with different team labels go through the same function and each request carries its own metadata.

source.title: Inference using Converse API - Amazon Bedrock

steps.why: A gateway is where a platform team centralises attribution, limits and model choice, and request metadata is how Bedrock carries that attribution into its logs.

steps.do: Create a guardrail, enable it in the gateway's Converse calls, and write an automated test with pinned SDK versions that asserts a blocked input is intercepted.
steps.done_when: The test passes from a clean environment and the response for the blocked input shows the guardrail intervened.

steps.why: A policy enforced in the gateway and checked by a repeatable test stays in force as prompts and models change. Pinning the environment makes the test give the same result on a laptop and in CI.

steps.do: Configure the gateway to call the model through an inference profile instead of a single-region model identifier, and rerun the full test suite.
steps.done_when: All tests pass with the inference profile identifier and the usage log still records tokens, latency and team metadata for every call.

verified.section_found: Use an inference profile in a conversation

steps.why: Inference profiles spread traffic across regions for higher throughput and resilience, which is how a production gateway avoids being bound to one region's quota.
